title: RT Level 2 Practice Questions 2026: Free 30-Question Mock Exam
metaDescription: Free RT Level II mock exam: 30 original radiographic testing questions with answers on physics, IQIs, exposure math, interpretation and radiation safety.
h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) Level II Practice Questions
intro: These 30 questions are original study questions written by Atlantis NDT for technicians preparing for Radiographic Testing (RT) Level II. They are not ASNT examination questions and do not reproduce any certification exam.

Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A (2024 edition), the employer certifies Level II personnel after general, specific and practical examinations set out in its written practice. ASNT also offers central ASNT NDT Level II examinations (general and method exams), and employers still carry out the vision, practical and job-specific examinations. This set is pitched at what a Level II must do: set up and verify the system, make the exposure, interpret and evaluate radiographs against a procedure, and report the results.

The questions cover radiation physics and sources, film, screens, IQIs and digital systems, exposure calculations, technique and code requirements, interpretation, and radiation safety. Atlantis NDT runs NDT training year-round, with theory online and practicals in its Practical NDT simulator or in person at the client's own facility.
howToUse: Answer each question before opening the explanation, and note the topic of every question you miss.
Work the calculations on paper; the explanations show each step so you can check your method.
Check code references against the edition your procedures and written practice actually use, since requirements can change between editions.
Study your weakest topics, then retake the full set a few days later without notes.

questions.q: When X-ray tube voltage (kV) is increased while tube current and exposure time stay the same, what is the main effect on the beam?
options: Intensity increases but the energy spectrum is unchanged
The spectrum shifts to shorter wavelengths, increasing penetration and reducing subject contrast
Subject contrast increases because more low-energy photons are produced
Only the effective focal spot size changes
questions.explanation: Higher kV raises the maximum and average photon energy (shorter wavelength), so the beam penetrates more and the difference in absorption between thicknesses falls, lowering subject contrast. Intensity also rises, but the first option is wrong because the spectrum does change.

questions.q: Increasing X-ray tube current (mA) at a fixed kV mainly:
options: Shortens the wavelength of the beam
Increases the number of photons (intensity) without changing the photon energy range
questions.explanation: Tube current controls how many electrons strike the target, so intensity rises roughly in proportion to mA. The maximum energy and the shape of the spectrum are set by kV, not mA.

questions.q: What determines the energies of the gamma rays emitted by an Ir-192 source?
options: The radioactive isotope itself; the operator cannot adjust them
The activity of the source in curies or becquerels
The physical size of the source pellet
questions.explanation: Gamma-ray energies are characteristic of the decaying isotope. Activity sets how many photons are emitted per second (intensity), not their energy, and distance and source size affect intensity and unsharpness only.

questions.q: Which interaction is the main source of scattered radiation when steel is radiographed with Ir-192 or Co-60 gamma rays?
questions.explanation: In steel, Compton scattering is the dominant interaction across the gamma energies of Ir-192 and Co-60 and produces most of the scatter that degrades contrast. Pair production needs photon energies above 1.02 MeV and is minor at these energies, while photoelectric absorption dominates only at lower energies.

questions.q: Compared with Ir-192, Se-75 has:
options: Higher average gamma energy and a shorter half-life
Higher average gamma energy and a longer half-life
The same gamma energies but a shorter half-life
Lower average gamma energy and a longer half-life
questions.explanation: Se-75 emits lower-energy gamma rays than Ir-192, which gives better contrast on thinner steel sections. Its half-life is about 120 days, compared with about 74 days for Ir-192.

topics.name: Film, screens, IQIs and digital systems

questions.q: What is the main function of lead intensifying screens in film radiography?
options: They emit light when struck by radiation, and the light exposes the film
They emit electrons when struck by radiation, intensifying the image, and the front screen also absorbs some lower-energy scatter
They allow a lower kV to be used regardless of material thickness
They remove the need for an image quality indicator
questions.explanation: Lead screens release electrons that add to the film exposure, and the front screen preferentially absorbs lower-energy scattered radiation. Screens that emit light are fluorescent screens, which are a different type.

questions.q: Two films are exposed to the same density. Compared with a fast, coarse-grain film, a slow, fine-grain film gives:
options: Higher definition and lower graininess, but needs a longer exposure
Lower definition and a shorter exposure
Higher graininess and a shorter exposure
The same definition with a shorter exposure
questions.explanation: Finer grain gives better definition and lower graininess but lower film speed, so more exposure is needed to reach the same density. This is why slower films are chosen where high sensitivity is required.

questions.q: On a wire-type image quality indicator (IQI), the essential wire is:
options: Always the thickest wire in the set
The wire placed closest to the film identification
The wire specified for the material thickness, which must be visible in the area of interest to show the required sensitivity
Any wire that happens to be visible on the radiograph
questions.explanation: The code or procedure designates the wire diameter for the thickness being radiographed, and seeing that wire shows the required sensitivity was achieved. Seeing only thicker wires means the requirement was not met.
questions.ref: ASTM E747; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 2

questions.q: A hole-type (plaque) IQI sensitivity level is stated as 2-2T. What does this mean?
options: Two plaques must be used, each 2 mm thick
The plaque is 2 mm thick and any two holes must be visible
The radiograph must show a 2% density difference across two holes
The plaque thickness is 2% of the part thickness and the hole with a diameter twice the plaque thickness must be visible
questions.explanation: In the hole-type IQI system, the first number is plaque thickness as a percentage of part thickness and the second is the hole that must be seen (1T, 2T or 4T). 2-2T is a commonly specified level and corresponds to an equivalent sensitivity of 2%.
questions.ref: ASTM E1025; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 2

questions.q: Why is the IQI normally placed on the source side of the part when access allows?
options: Because film-side placement is never permitted by any code
Because the source side is farthest from the film, so unsharpness is greatest there and the IQI shows sensitivity under the least favorable conditions
Because the IQI shields the film from backscatter
Because source-side placement shortens the exposure time
questions.explanation: Features farthest from the film are imaged with the most geometric unsharpness, so a source-side IQI is the stricter check. Film-side placement is allowed when the source side is inaccessible, with the identification the procedure requires.
questions.ref: General RT principle; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 2

questions.q: In computed radiography (CR), the latent image is stored in:
options: A silver halide emulsion that is developed chemically
An amorphous silicon flat panel that is read out directly after exposure
A photostimulable phosphor imaging plate that is read out by a laser scanner
A fluorescent screen viewed in real time by a camera
questions.explanation: CR uses reusable phosphor imaging plates that hold the latent image until a scanning laser releases it as light for digitizing. A flat panel read out directly is a digital detector array (DDA), a different technology.

questions.q: Source size 3 mm, source-to-object distance 600 mm, object-to-film distance 25 mm. Using Ug = F·d/D, what is the geometric unsharpness?
questions.explanation: Ug = F × d / D = 3 × 25 / 600 = 0.125 mm, where F is the effective source or focal spot size, d is the object-to-film distance and D is the source-to-object distance.
questions.ref: General RT principle; ASME BPVC Section V, Article 2

questions.q: A satisfactory exposure takes 2 minutes at a source-to-film distance of 600 mm. With everything else unchanged, what exposure time gives the same density at 900 mm?
questions.explanation: Exposure time is proportional to the square of the distance: 2 × (900/600)² = 2 × 2.25 = 4.5 min. A linear correction (3.0 min) would under-expose the film.

questions.q: An acceptable exposure was made at 10 mA for 2 minutes. The X-ray set must now run at 5 mA at the same kV and distance. What exposure time gives the same density?
questions.explanation: At fixed kV and distance, the exposure in mA·min is kept constant: 10 × 2 = 20 mA·min, so 20 / 5 = 4 min.

questions.q: An Ir-192 source has an activity of 3,700 GBq (100 Ci) today. Taking the half-life as 74 days, what is its approximate activity after 148 days?
questions.explanation: 148 days is two half-lives, so the activity falls to one quarter: 3,700 / 4 = 925 GBq (25 Ci).

questions.q: An exposure with a Se-75 source took 8 minutes. Taking the half-life as 120 days, what exposure time is needed for the same setup 240 days later?
questions.explanation: 240 days is two half-lives, so the activity is one quarter of the original and the exposure time must be four times longer: 8 × 4 = 32 min.

questions.q: From the film's characteristic curve, the log relative exposure needed for the target density is 0.3 higher than the log relative exposure used. By roughly what factor must the exposure be multiplied?
questions.explanation: A difference of 0.3 in log E corresponds to a factor of 10^0.3, which is about 2, so the exposure (for example in mA·min) must be roughly doubled.

questions.q: The source is outside a pipe, radiation passes through both walls, and only the wall nearest the film is evaluated. This technique is:
questions.explanation: In DWSI the source-side wall is far from the film and too unsharp to interpret, so only the film-side wall is evaluated. In DWDI both walls are evaluated on the same image.

questions.q: Why is the source offset from the weld plane when making a double-wall double-image (elliptical) exposure of a small-diameter pipe weld?
options: To avoid the need for an IQI
To place the film-side weld closer to the source
To separate the images of the source-side and film-side welds so both can be evaluated without overlap
questions.explanation: Offsetting the source projects the two weld images as an ellipse instead of one on top of the other. A superimposed (non-offset) technique can also be used, but the images overlap and more exposures are then needed to cover the circumference.

questions.q: A lead letter 'B' is attached to the back of the film holder. The processed radiograph shows a light image of the 'B' on a darker background. Under ASME Section V Article 2, this means:
options: Backscatter protection was insufficient and the radiograph is unacceptable
The IQI was placed on the wrong side
questions.explanation: A light 'B' shows that backscattered radiation reached the film around the letter, so backscatter protection was inadequate and the radiograph is rejected. A dark 'B' on a lighter background is not a cause for rejection.

questions.q: For single-film viewing of a radiograph made with an X-ray source, ASME Section V Article 2 requires the density through the body of the IQI and the area of interest to be within which range?
questions.explanation: For single-film viewing, the Article 2 limits are 1.8 to 4.0 for X-ray radiographs and 2.0 to 4.0 for gamma-ray radiographs. Composite viewing of two films has separate limits.

questions.q: When the IQI cannot be placed on the source side and is placed on the film side, ASME Section V Article 2 requires:
options: A lead letter 'F' placed adjacent to or on the IQI
A second IQI on the source side
A lead letter 'B' on the front of the film holder
questions.explanation: The lead 'F' tells the interpreter that the IQI was on the film side. This matters because a film-side IQI is imaged more sharply than it would be on the source side.

questions.q: An area of a processed film transmits 1% of the incident light from the viewer. What is its film density?
questions.explanation: Density D = log10(I0 / It) = log10(100 / 1) = 2.0.

questions.q: Small, rounded, sharply defined dark spots scattered through the weld metal on a radiograph are most typical of:
questions.explanation: Gas pores contain little or no metal, so they appear as rounded areas of higher density (darker). Tungsten inclusions appear lighter than the weld because tungsten is denser than steel.

questions.q: On a radiograph of a GTAW steel weld, a very light (low-density), sharply defined irregular spot most likely indicates:
questions.explanation: Tungsten absorbs far more radiation than steel, so a tungsten inclusion appears as a light spot. Porosity and slag are less dense than steel and appear darker.

questions.q: In a single-V butt weld, a straight, dark, continuous line along the center of the root, often with sharp parallel edges, most likely indicates:
questions.explanation: Unfused root faces leave a narrow gap along the joint centerline, imaged as a straight dark line. Lack of sidewall fusion usually lies off-center along a bevel face, and excessive root reinforcement appears lighter, not darker.

questions.q: A suspected linear indication is seen on a radiograph. Which observation best suggests it is a film-handling artifact rather than a discontinuity in the part?
options: It appears darker than the surrounding weld
It runs parallel to the weld axis
It is close to the IQI
Under reflected light, the emulsion surface is visibly scratched or marked at the same location
questions.explanation: Viewing the film surface in reflected light reveals scratches, pressure marks and similar damage to the emulsion. Real discontinuities are in the part and do not mark the emulsion; darkness and orientation alone do not separate the two.

questions.q: A survey meter reads 80 µSv/h at 2 m from an unshielded gamma source. Using the inverse square law, what is the approximate dose rate at 8 m?
questions.explanation: Dose rate falls with the square of distance: 80 × (2/8)² = 80 / 16 = 5 µSv/h. Four times the distance gives one sixteenth of the dose rate, not one quarter.

questions.q: The half-value layer (HVL) of a shielding material for a given source is 12 mm. What thickness reduces the dose rate to one eighth of its unshielded value?
questions.explanation: Each HVL halves the dose rate, and one eighth is (1/2)³, so three HVLs are needed: 3 × 12 = 36 mm. This is the simple narrow-beam calculation; scatter in real shielding means designs add margin.

questions.q: Why must a calibrated survey meter be used when approaching a gamma exposure device after every exposure?
options: To confirm the source has returned fully to its shielded position
To replace the need for a personal dosimeter
To check the source activity for the exposure calculation
questions.explanation: A survey on every approach is the direct check that the source is back in the shielded position, and failing to survey is a well-known cause of radiography overexposure incidents. Personal dosimeters record dose but do not replace the survey.
